introduction_markdown: GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0755 Geology 1, JUNE 2022, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, 1 hour 30 minutes. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0755 GEOLOGY - 1'; fill in the information required in the spaces above and on the answer sheet (Candidate Number, Name, Centre Number and Name). Answer ALL the 50 questions. All questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is correct, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet, using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet.

questions.enonce_markdown: The totality of space and time, past, present and future, consisting of millions of stars clustered in galaxies is the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Universe is the totality of space, time, matter and energy, including all galaxies and the billions of stars they contain. The Big Bang theory is only a model for how the Universe began, the Solar system is the Sun with the bodies that orbit it (a tiny part of one galaxy), and a planet is a single body orbiting a star.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a terrestrial planet?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Terrestrial (rocky) planets are the four inner planets Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars: small, dense, with solid silicate crusts. Saturn, Neptune and Uranus are giant (Jovian) planets made mostly of hydrogen, helium and ices.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 1 below shows the upper part of the internal structure of the Earth. Use it to answer questions 3 and 4.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: upper part of the internal structure of the Earth (depth marks 0 km, 70 km, 200 km and 670 km; continental crust and oceanic crust; X is the interval from 0 to 70 km, Y the interval from 70 to 200 km; an arrow from the right points to a boundary at the base of the oceanic crust).*

What do X and Y represent respectively?
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the diagram X spans the depth interval from 0 km to the 70 km mark: this is the rigid outer shell made of the crust and the uppermost rigid mantle, the **lithosphere**. Y spans the interval from the 70 km mark to the 200 km mark, the weak, partly molten and plastic layer beneath it, the **asthenosphere**, on which the lithospheric plates move. The mantle and the outer core lie much deeper (the outer core begins at about 2900 km).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 1 (the same figure as for question 3).

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: upper part of the internal structure of the Earth (depth marks 0 km, 70 km, 200 km and 670 km; continental crust and oceanic crust; X is the interval from 0 to 70 km, Y the interval from 70 to 200 km; an arrow from the right points to a boundary at the base of the oceanic crust).*

Which boundary occurs at N?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The arrow drawn from the right of Figure 1 points to the boundary at the base of the crust (here under the thin oceanic crust). The boundary between the crust and the mantle is the **Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho)**. The Gutenberg discontinuity is the mantle-outer core boundary at about 2900 km, and the Conrad discontinuity is the boundary inside the continental crust between its upper (granitic) and lower (basaltic) parts.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Earthquakes that are responsible for giant sea waves on the ocean floor are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor during a submarine earthquake sets the overlying water in motion and produces giant sea waves called **tsunamis**. Seismic waves and body waves are the vibrations that travel through the Earth, not the sea waves themselves.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Seismic waves that are propagated through the Earth as a series of compressions and expansions are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Primary (P) waves** are longitudinal (compressional) waves: particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, producing alternate compressions and expansions. They are the fastest seismic waves and travel through solids and liquids. Secondary (S) waves are transverse shear waves, Rayleigh waves are surface waves with rolling motion, and 'body waves' is the general name for both P and S waves, so it is not the specific answer.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following forms occurs in crystals of the cubic system?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The forms of the cubic (isometric) system include the cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and, in the hextetrahedral class, the **tetrahedron** (for example in sphalerite and tetrahedrite). A basal pinacoid, prisms and pyramids need a unique principal axis c that differs from the other axes (tetragonal, hexagonal and orthorhombic systems) and do not occur as forms of the cubic system.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystallographic axes below (Figure 2) and answer questions 8 and 9.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: crystallographic axes (a vertical axis +a3/-a3, a horizontal axis -a2/+a2 and an inclined axis -a1 at the upper right, +a2 printed at the lower left).*

State the axial angles between the crystallographic axes:

*Options as printed:* A) $a = b = c$ that is $\alpha = \beta = 90^\circ \delta$   B) $a = b \neq c$ that is $\alpha = \beta = \delta = 90^\circ$   C) $a = b = c$ that is $\alpha = \beta = \delta = 90^\circ$   D) $a \neq b \neq c$ that is $\alpha \neq \beta = \delta \neq 90^\circ$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The three axes of the figure are mutually perpendicular and, in the cubic system they represent, they have equal lengths: $a = b = c$ with all interaxial angles equal to $90^\circ$ ($\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ$; the paper writes the third angle as $\delta$). Option B ($a = b \neq c$) is the tetragonal system, option D has unequal angles and is not perpendicular (triclinic), and option A, as printed, gives only two of the three angles.

**Intended answer: C ($a = b = c$ that is $\alpha = \beta = \delta = 90^\circ$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 2 (the same figure as for question 8).

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: crystallographic axes (a vertical axis +a3/-a3, a horizontal axis -a2/+a2 and an inclined axis -a1 at the upper right, +a2 printed at the lower left).*

Which crystal system is represented by the crystallographic axes above?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The figure shows three axes of the same kind, named $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$ (all called $a$, because they are equal in length), at right angles to each other. Three equal axes at $90^\circ$ define the **cubic system**. The tetragonal system has two equal axes and a different third axis $c$, the monoclinic system has one oblique angle and the triclinic system has three oblique angles.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Give an example of a phyllosilicate:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Phyllosilicates are sheet silicates, built of linked SiO4 tetrahedra forming sheets, which explains their perfect basal cleavage into thin flakes. The micas (muscovite, biotite), the clay minerals, chlorite and talc belong to this group. Pyroxene is a single-chain silicate, amphibole a double-chain silicate and orthoclase a framework silicate (feldspar).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
From which of these minerals can a good quantity of copper be extracted?

*Options as printed:* A) Pyrite   B) Azurite   C) Malachite   D) Chalcopyrite
questions.corrige_markdown:
Pyrite ($\mathrm{FeS_2}$) is an iron sulphide and contains no copper. The other three are all copper minerals: chalcopyrite ($\mathrm{CuFeS_2}$, about 35 % Cu) is the commonest and most important copper ore worldwide, while malachite (about 57 % Cu) and azurite (about 55 % Cu) are copper carbonates that contain a higher proportion of copper but are usually found in smaller quantities in the oxidised zone. The question does not say whether 'a good quantity' refers to the percentage of copper in the mineral or to the amount of copper mined, so the printed question is ambiguous.

**Intended answer: D (Chalcopyrite).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following factors influences the hardness of a mineral?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hardness measures resistance to scratching and depends on the strength of the chemical bonds in the crystal structure. The main controls are the **ionic radius** (the smaller the ions, the shorter and stronger the bonds, so the harder the mineral), the ionic charge, the type of bonding and how tightly the atoms are packed. Heavy ions as such, the direction of the bonds and parting planes (which are planes of weakness that affect breakage, not scratch hardness) are not recognised controls of hardness.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Bonds placed in the same direction

questions.enonce_markdown: Cemented volcanic ash are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Volcanic ash (fragments smaller than 2 mm) that has been compacted and cemented forms a rock called **tuff**. Agglomerates are made of large rounded volcanic bombs (over 64 mm), ignimbrites are welded deposits of pyroclastic flows and scoria is vesicular basaltic lava or cinder, not cemented ash.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram below (Figure 3) to answer question 14.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: block diagram of tilted beds (conglomerate, sandstone, limestone, shale, marl) with a tilted igneous body marked X, and a key.*

What is the igneous feature X called?

*Options as printed:* A) Dyke   B) Sill   C) Batholith   D) Bed
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Figure 3 the igneous body marked X lies between sedimentary beds and has the same strike and the same steep dip as them: it is **concordant** (parallel to the bedding), a sheet-like intrusion, and therefore a **sill** (here tilted with the beds). A dyke would cut across the beds (discordant), a batholith is a very large irregular body and a bed is a sedimentary layer. Some textbooks nevertheless call a steeply inclined sheet a dyke, so the key cannot be fixed with certainty from the sketch.

**Intended answer: B (Sill).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following landforms can be produced by both quiet and violent eruptions?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **composite volcano** (strato-volcano) is built by alternating quiet effusions of lava and violent explosive eruptions of ash and pyroclasts, so it records both types of eruption. Ash and cinder cones are formed by explosive eruptions only, and volcanic or lava domes are formed by very viscous lava that piles up above the vent.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
An acid igneous rock which contains quartz and calc-alkali feldspar as essential minerals is a/an:

*Options as printed:* A) Granite   B) Granodiorite   C) Rhyolite   D) Obsidian
questions.corrige_markdown:
An acid rock has more than 65 % silica and contains quartz. Granite is the classic acid plutonic rock whose essential minerals are quartz and alkali (calc-alkali) feldspar (orthoclase, microcline) with biotite or muscovite. Granodiorite has plagioclase dominant over alkali feldspar, and obsidian is a volcanic glass without crystals. Rhyolite, the volcanic equivalent of granite, has the same essential minerals but as fine grains or phenocrysts, so the printed question does not exclude it.

**Intended answer: A (Granite).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A texture exhibited by igneous rocks having large augite crystals partially or wholly enclosing small plagioclase crystals is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In **ophitic** texture (typical of dolerite) laths of plagioclase are partly or wholly enclosed in larger crystals of augite. A porphyritic texture is large crystals in a fine groundmass, a graphic texture is an intergrowth of quartz and feldspar that looks like writing, and a poikilitic texture is one large crystal enclosing many small randomly oriented crystals of another mineral without the lath-shaped relation described here.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An igneous rock formed when lava solidifies into a fine grained black rock is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Basalt** is the dark (black to dark grey), fine-grained extrusive rock formed when basic lava cools quickly at the surface. Rhyolite is a light-coloured acid extrusive rock, pumice is a light frothy glass and gabbro is the coarse-grained intrusive equivalent of basalt.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The chemical weathering process which converts anhydrite into gypsum is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Anhydrite ($\mathrm{CaSO_4}$) takes up water into its crystal structure to form gypsum ($\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$), with an increase in volume. The addition of water molecules without breaking down the mineral is **hydration**. Hydrolysis is a reaction with the $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ions of water that changes the mineral into a new one (for example feldspar into clay).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When water in a volcanic area is heated underground and flows to the surface it forms what are known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Groundwater heated by hot rocks or magma that flows steadily to the surface forms **hot springs**. A geyser is a special case in which the heated water and steam are ejected intermittently as a jet, so it does not simply 'flow'. Ordinary springs are cold, and grikes and clints are limestone pavement features.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A feature formed in a karst area by river erosion and the collapse of a cave roof is called a:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In limestone country a river may flow through a cave. When the roof of the cave collapses, the river is left in a deep, steep-sided valley, a **gorge** (for example the Cheddar Gorge). A doline and a sinkhole are hollows formed by solution or by collapse above underground drainage, not by a river, and a grike is a solution-widened joint in a limestone pavement.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A student analysed a detrital rock sample as follows: 25% pebble sized particles; 70% sand sized particles and 50% reddish brown fine binding material. Use this description to answer questions 22, 23 and 24.

The most likely name given to this rock is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The rock is dominated by sand-sized grains (70 %), with a significant proportion (25 %) of pebbles. A sandstone with scattered pebbles is a **pebbly sandstone**. A conglomerate needs the pebbles to be the dominant grains, and the description gives no information about the size of the sand grains (coarse or medium). The percentages as printed add up to more than 100 % (the binding material is printed as 50 %, probably 5 %), but the sand grains and pebbles dominate in either reading.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A student analysed a detrital rock sample as follows: 25% pebble sized particles; 70% sand sized particles and 50% reddish brown fine binding material. Use this description to answer questions 22, 23 and 24.

What is the composition of the binding material?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A reddish brown fine cement is coloured by ferric iron: the binding material is **iron oxide** (haematite), which gives red sandstones their colour. Silica and calcite cements are white, colourless or pale, and limonite is a yellow-brown hydrated iron oxide mineral, not the general composition asked for.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A student analysed a detrital rock sample as follows: 25% pebble sized particles; 70% sand sized particles and 50% reddish brown fine binding material. Use this description to answer questions 22, 23 and 24.

What is the environment of deposition of the rock?

*Options as printed:* A) Deposition in a lagoon   B) Deposition in an arid environment   C) Deposition by turbidity currents   D) Deposition in piedmont
questions.corrige_markdown:
The red colour of the ferric iron cement shows that the sediment was exposed to oxygen and dried out, which is typical of hot, **arid** conditions (red beds, desert and dry-land deposits). Lagoon deposits are generally fine and grey, and turbidity currents give graded greywackes. A piedmont (alluvial fan) setting is also possible in an arid climate and can produce red pebbly sands, so the printed question is open to a second reading.

**Intended answer: B (Deposition in an arid environment).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: All the features, textures and structures in a metamorphic rock could collectively be described as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **fabric** of a rock is the sum of all its textures and structures: the size, shape and arrangement of its grains, foliation, lineation and so on. Relic structures are original features that survive metamorphism, preferred orientation is the alignment of minerals, and lineations are linear features only.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A sandy limestone recrystallizes during contact metamorphism into:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Pure limestone becomes pure (calcite) marble. When the limestone contains silica (sand), calcite reacts with quartz at high temperature: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3 + CO_2}$, giving **wollastonite marble**. Brucite and forsterite marbles come from magnesium-rich (dolomitic) limestones.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is regarded as a high grade metamorphic rock?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Metamorphic grade increases in the sequence slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss. **Gneiss** forms at high temperature and pressure and is the high-grade rock. Slate and phyllite are low-grade, and green schist belongs to the low to medium-grade greenschist facies.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 4) that shows different types of plate boundaries. Use it to answer questions 28 and 29.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: plate boundaries (a mid oceanic ridge on the left, an oceanic plate descending beneath a continental plate on the right with partial melting; X marks the oceanic plate, Y the zone where it descends).*

Identify the type(s) of plate boundary shown on the diagram.
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the left the mid oceanic ridge is a **constructive** (divergent) boundary where new oceanic crust is created. On the right the oceanic plate descends beneath the continental plate with partial melting, a **destructive** (convergent, subduction) boundary. The question asks for the type(s) shown, so both must be named. Option B describes only the subduction boundary, and the figure shows no ocean-ocean or continent-continent collision.

**Answer: D.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 4 (the same figure as for question 28).

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: plate boundaries (a mid oceanic ridge on the left, an oceanic plate descending beneath a continental plate on the right with partial melting; X marks the oceanic plate, Y the zone where it descends).*

What type of metamorphism will likely occur at Y?

*Options as printed:* A) Contact   B) Regional   C) Dynamic   D) Dynamothermal
questions.corrige_markdown:
Y marks the zone where the descending oceanic plate meets the overriding continental plate. Along a subduction zone and the mountain belt above it, rocks are subjected to high pressure and rising temperature over a large area, the conditions of **regional metamorphism** (the usual textbook answer for convergent plate boundaries). Contact metamorphism is local, around an intrusion, and dynamic metamorphism affects narrow fault zones. As the exact position of Y on the sketch is unclear, and dynamothermal metamorphism is a related term for regional metamorphism, the key is uncertain.

**Intended answer: B (Regional).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
A student on fieldwork in Mabanda, Kumba encountered a granite outcrop with a set of joints more or less parallel to the topographic surface. Use this information to answer question 30.

What is the mode of formation of the joints above?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Joints parallel to the ground surface in granite are **sheet joints** (exfoliation joints). A deep-seated granite is under great confining pressure; when erosion removes the overburden the pressure is released (unloading), the rock expands upwards and cracks parallel to the surface. Contraction on cooling gives columnar or polygonal joints, folding and thrusting give joints related to fold axes, and tension joints are not surface-parallel.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Contraction towards a number of cooling centres.
Folding and thrusting caused by tectonic movements.
Tensional forces set up within the rock.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram of a fault below (Figure 5) and answer questions 31, 32 and 33.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: section of a fault cutting two beds (X is the horizontal dashed distance, Y the vertical dashed distance between the displaced beds).*

The letters X and Y respectively represent?
questions.corrige_markdown:
X is the horizontal displacement of the bed across the fault, the **heave**; Y is the vertical displacement, the **throw**. The net-slip is measured along the fault plane itself and the hade is the angle between the fault plane and the vertical, neither of which is drawn as a horizontal or vertical dashed line.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 5 (the same figure as for question 31).

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: section of a fault cutting two beds (X is the horizontal dashed distance, Y the vertical dashed distance between the displaced beds).*

The above fault can be best described as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The fault plane dips to the right, so the block on the right is the hanging wall (above the fault plane). The beds in this block lie lower than the same beds in the footwall, so the hanging wall has moved down relative to the footwall: a **normal fault**, produced by tension (extension, with a horizontal heave that widens the crust). Strike-slip (wrench) faults show horizontal movement and a reverse fault would have the hanging wall moved up.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The classification of folds based on the mode of formation is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A classification based on how a fold formed (for example by buckling, flexure, flow or drag) is a **genetic classification**. Geometric classifications describe the shape of the fold (interlimb angle, closing direction and so on), not its origin.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram of the fossil below (Figure 6) and answer questions 34 and 35.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

*Figure 6: coiled fossil shell with radial dotted lines in the inner part; lines X (from the outside to the middle of the outer whorl) and Y (from the right to the inner whorl).*

Name the group of fossils represented by the diagram above.

*Options as printed:* A) Nautiloids   B) Gonatites   C) Ceratites   D) Ammonites
questions.corrige_markdown:
The fossil is a planispirally coiled, chambered cephalopod shell, with the chambers shown by radial septa. This is the typical outline drawn for the ammonoids, the **ammonites**. Nautiloids also coil, but the figure is a simple sketch and does not show the suture pattern (goniatite, ceratite or ammonite type) or the siphuncle position, so the choice between the four printed groups cannot be proved from the diagram.

**Intended answer: D (Ammonites).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 6 (the same figure as for question 34).

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

*Figure 6: coiled fossil shell with radial dotted lines in the inner part; lines X (from the outside to the middle of the outer whorl) and Y (from the right to the inner whorl).*

Label the part marked X.

*Options as printed:* A) Saddles   B) Lobes   C) Umbilicus   D) Whorl
questions.corrige_markdown:
The line X starts outside the shell, crosses the shell wall and ends inside the large outer coil, the chamber-bearing turn of the shell: this part is a **whorl**. The umbilicus is the central depression at the middle of the coil, and saddles and lobes are the crests and troughs of the suture lines on the septa, which are not marked by X. The line ends close to the centre of the coil, so the label could also be read as the umbilicus.

**Intended answer: D (Whorl).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The contact representing missing rock strata separating beds that are parallel to one another is called a parallel unconformity or:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **disconformity** is an unconformity in which the beds above and below the surface of erosion are parallel, and strata are missing: it is also called a parallel unconformity. A paraconformity is a similar parallel contact but with no visible erosion surface, a nonconformity has sedimentary rocks lying on igneous or metamorphic rocks, and a heterolithic unconformity has different rock types on either side.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Time equivalence of rock units in different areas is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Showing that rock units in different places were formed at the same time (using fossils, rock type or marker beds) is **correlation**. Absolute dating gives an age in years, relative dating only gives the order of events, and an unconformity is a break in the record.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram below (Figure 7) to answer question 38.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

*Figure 7: a vertical sequence of beds a (marine), b (swamp), c (deltaic), d (lagoonal), c (deltaic), b (swamp), a (marine) from top to bottom.*

Identify the type of cyclotherm shown on the diagram.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Reading the column from the bottom: marine (a), swamp (b), deltaic (c), lagoonal (d), then deltaic (c), swamp (b), marine (a) again. The sequence reverses on both sides of the central bed d, so it is **symmetrical**: this is a cyclic cyclotherm (a transgression up to bed d followed by a regression). A rhythmic cyclotherm repeats the same sequence in the same order (a, b, c, d, a, b, c, d). Transgression and regression describe the direction of the shoreline, not the type of cyclotherm.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Any naturally occurring body of mineral or rock that is of economic value and can be worked at a profit is a/an:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A body of mineral or rock that can be mined at a profit is an **ore deposit**. A mineral deposit is any concentration of a mineral, whether or not it can be worked at a profit, an ore mineral is the valuable mineral itself, and a gangue mineral is the worthless material found with the ore.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An accumulation of mechanically weathered mineral particles transported and deposited by running water is called a/an:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Heavy, resistant minerals (gold, cassiterite, diamond) released by weathering and concentrated by running water form a **placer deposit**. A residual deposit stays in place where it was formed by weathering and a secondary enrichment deposit is formed by downward-moving solutions.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The impermeable rock layer overlying an oil bearing stratum is a/an:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The impermeable layer that prevents oil from escaping upwards from the reservoir rock is the **cap rock** (seal). The oil trap is the whole structure, the oil field is the area of productive wells and the source rock is where the oil was formed.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A rock type which is commonly used for road construction in Cameroon is:

*Options as printed:* A) Slate   B) Gabbro   C) Granite   D) Basalt
questions.corrige_markdown:
Road aggregate must be hard, strong and durable. Slate splits into thin plates and is unsuitable, whereas gabbro, granite and basalt are all hard crystalline rocks that are quarried for road stone. In Cameroon granite and other basement rocks and the volcanic basalts of the Cameroon Volcanic Line are used, so the printed question has no single certain answer.

**Intended answer: C (Granite).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: engineering geology and quarry site selection

questions.enonce_markdown: A well in which the water encountered at depth is under a sufficient hydraulic pressure to force it up to the surface is a/an:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In an **artesian well** the water comes from a confined aquifer, held between impermeable layers, and the hydraulic pressure forces it up to the surface without pumping. A perched water table and an unconfined aquifer are not under pressure, and 'natural well' is not a hydrogeological term.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The most poisonous gas emitted from lake Nyos in Cameroon, killing people, livestock and displacing people in 1986 was:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In August 1986 a huge cloud of **carbon dioxide** that had accumulated in the deep water of the crater lake Nyos was suddenly released (a limnic eruption). The gas is denser than air, flowed down the valleys and suffocated about 1,700 people and many animals. The other gases are not the main gas of the disaster.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following is a secondary volcanic hazard?

*Options as printed:* A) Landslide   B) Soil creep   C) Earthquake   D) Lahar
questions.corrige_markdown:
Primary hazards are produced directly by the eruption (lava, ash fall, pyroclastic flows, gases). Secondary hazards follow from it: **lahars** (volcanic mudflows of ash and water), floods, tsunamis and landslides. Both a lahar and a landslide on a volcano can be secondary hazards, so the printed question has two defensible options; the lahar is the classic example. Soil creep and earthquakes are not secondary hazards of a volcano in the usual lists.

**Intended answer: D (Lahar).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cameroon Volcanic Line (CVL) is characterised by the presence of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The CVL is a chain of volcanoes, ring complexes and volcanic plateaus (Mount Cameroon, Manengouba, Bamenda highlands, Mandara and others) whose volcanic rocks are mostly of **Tertiary to Quaternary** age. The Precambrian basement lies beneath and beside the line but is not the characteristic of the line, and no Palaeozoic volcanic rocks are involved.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The oil and gas fields in Cameroon are located in the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The producing oil and gas fields of Cameroon lie offshore and near shore in the Atlantic coastal basins, mainly the **Rio del Rey Basin** (with the Douala/Kribi-Campo basin for gas). The Doba Basin is in Chad (its oil is exported through Cameroon) and the Logone-Birni Basin is an inland basin in the north without production, and the CVL is a volcanic chain, not a hydrocarbon province.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Geologic section (Figure 8) below shows rocks and their contacts with each other. Use it to answer questions 48 to 50.

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: geologic section A-B with igneous rock, shale, limestone, pebbly sand, marl and sandstone; the structure M-M cuts the dipping beds.*

Identify the geologic structure labelled M - M.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The line M - M cuts through the dipping beds, and the beds on its two sides (shale, marl and sandstone) do not meet: the same bands are displaced relative to one another. A fracture with displacement is a **fault**. A joint is a fracture without displacement, an unconformity is a surface of erosion or non-deposition between older and younger rocks (here the limestone surface at the top), and the line is not a river valley.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 8 (the same figure as for question 48).

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: geologic section A-B with igneous rock, shale, limestone, pebbly sand, marl and sandstone; the structure M-M cuts the dipping beds.*

What is the relationship between the igneous rocks and the overlying limestone?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The limestone rests on a surface of erosion cut into the igneous rock: a surface of erosion with younger sedimentary rock on older igneous (plutonic) rock is a **nonconformity**. An angular unconformity is between tilted and flat-lying sedimentary beds (this is the relation of the limestone to the dipping sedimentary beds), and a disconformity is between parallel sedimentary beds.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 8 (the same figure as for questions 48 and 49).

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2022-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: geologic section A-B with igneous rock, shale, limestone, pebbly sand, marl and sandstone; the structure M-M cuts the dipping beds.*

The oldest bed in the area is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the key the units are listed from the youngest (shale at the top) to the oldest (sandstone at the bottom). The igneous rock intrudes the dipping beds, so it is younger than the beds it cuts, and the horizontal limestone and shale lie across the eroded tilted beds, so they are younger still. The oldest bed is therefore the **sandstone**.

**Answer: C.**
